bib.title: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Chapter 5: Neural Networks

question: How should feed-forward neural networks be defined, trained by maximum likelihood with backpropagation, regularized, extended to multimodal targets and treated in a Bayesian way?
contributions: Backpropagation for gradients, Jacobian and Hessian (Sec 5.3-5.4)
Regularization: weight decay, early stopping, invariances, tangent propagation, convolutional nets, soft weight sharing (Sec 5.5)
Laplace-approximation Bayesian networks with evidence framework (Sec 5.7)

results.claim: Every point in weight space of a two-layer tanh network with M hidden units belongs to a family of M!2^M equivalent weight vectors (M! orderings times 2^M sign flips).
results.setup: Fully connected two-layer network, tanh hidden units, M hidden units; more layers multiply one factor per hidden layer.
results.quote: The network will therefore have an overall weight-space symmetry factor of M!2M.
results.note: Superscript flattened in the text: M!2M means M! x 2^M.

results.claim: Numerical differentiation loses the O(W) cost of backpropagation: each of W weights needs its own O(W) forward pass, so cost is O(W^2).
results.setup: W = total weights and biases; forward pass costs O(W).
results.quote: O(W) scaling has been lost

results.claim: Gradient evaluation by backpropagation costs O(W) steps per evaluation.
results.setup: Layered feed-forward network, W weights and biases, one input pattern.
results.quote: each such evaluation takes only O(W) steps

results.claim: Without gradient information, finding the minimum of the local quadratic needs O(W^2) function evaluations of O(W) each, so O(W^3) in total.
results.metric: cost to find minimum without gradients
results.setup: Quadratic approximation, which has O(W^2) free parameters.
results.quote: using such an approach would be O(W 3)

results.claim: With backpropagated gradients the minimum can be found in O(W^2) steps, which is why gradient information underlies practical training.
results.metric: cost to find minimum with gradients
results.setup: Same quadratic argument; O(W) gradient evaluations at O(W) each.
results.quote: the minimum can now be found in O(W 2) steps

results.claim: The local quadratic approximation b and H has W(W+3)/2 independent elements.
results.setup: W = number of adaptive parameters; H symmetric.
results.quote: the number of independent elements in the quadratic error function (5.28) is given by W(W + 3)/2.
results.note: Text p. 239 line-breaks the expression as 'W(W +' / '3)/2'.
results.where: p. 288, Exercise 5.13 (stated in text p. 239 as 'a total of W(W + 3)/2 independent elements')

results.claim: Central differences have O(eps^2) error versus O(eps) for forward differences, at roughly double the cost; the book says to use them to check a backprop implementation.
results.setup: Finite-difference check of backprop derivatives, eps << 1.
results.quote: the residual corrections are O(ϵ2)

results.claim: The exact Hessian of a feed-forward network can be computed in O(W^2) steps by extended backpropagation.
results.setup: Arbitrary feed-forward topology, any differentiable error and activation (Bishop 1991, 1992).
results.quote:
The number of computational steps needed to evaluate the Hessian scales
like O(W 2).

results.claim: The diagonal approximation of the Hessian costs O(W), versus O(W^2) for the full Hessian, but the true Hessian is typically strongly nondiagonal.
results.setup: Neglecting off-diagonal second-derivative terms (Becker and Le Cun 1989; Le Cun et al. 1990).
results.quote:
Note that the number of computational steps required to evaluate this approximation
is O(W)

results.claim: Finite-difference Hessian by perturbing pairs of weights costs O(W^3); applying central differences to backprop gradients costs O(W^2).
results.setup: Four forward propagations per element, W^2 elements.
results.quote: this approach will require O(W 3) operations to evaluate the complete Hessian

results.setup: Pearlmutter 1994; Moller 1993; two-layer example, linear outputs, sum-of-squares.

limits: Chapter has no experiments with reported test accuracies; figures are qualitative toy illustrations (sinusoid, 2-D synthetic classes, Appendix A) with no seeds or error tables.

Written in 2006: sigmoidal tanh/logistic hidden units, sum-of-squares or cross-entropy, batch methods (conjugate gradients, quasi-Newton, scaled conjugate gradient) preferred; no ReLU, dropout, batch norm, residual connections, Adam or minibatch SGD practice, no attention or transformers, no deep stacks.
Convolutional networks are covered in about two pages using average-subsampling units with sigmoid, not max pooling or ReLU.
Says plain gradient descent 'turns out to be a poor algorithm' for batch optimization; modern minibatch SGD practice differs.
Laplace evidence needs the Hessian determinant, which the author notes is sensitive to small eigenvalues that are hard to determine accurately.
Gradient descent is dismissed only by reference to Bishop and Nabney (2008), not argued here.
practices: Use identity outputs with sum-of-squares for regression, logistic sigmoid with cross-entropy for independent binary labels, softmax with multiclass cross-entropy for K exclusive classes; all give dE/da_k = y_k - t_k (Sec 5.2, pp. 235-236).
Call Fig 5.1 a two-layer network, counting layers of adaptive weights (p. 229).
Verify a backpropagation implementation against central differences (5.69) on some test cases, but train with backprop (p. 247).
Run a gradient optimiser several times from random starts and compare on an independent validation set (p. 240, Fig 5.10).
Use on-line (stochastic) gradient descent on large or redundant data sets; it handles redundancy well and can escape local minima (pp. 240-241).
Choose hidden units M by validation error, or use large M with a regulariser (pp. 256-257).
Use early stopping at the minimum validation error (p. 259, Fig 5.12).
Prefer regularizers invariant to linear rescaling: separate coefficients per layer, no biases (p. 258).
Encourage invariance by augmenting data with transformed copies, by tangent propagation, by invariant features, or by weight sharing (pp. 261-262).
Parametrise sigma^2 = exp(eta) and mixing coefficients by softmax to keep them valid (pp. 271, 274).
Use a mixture density network when p(t|x) is multimodal; use the mean of the most probable component as a mode estimate (p. 277).

terms.definition: 'multilayer perceptron' is really a misnomer, because the model comprises multiple layers of logistic regression models (with continuous nonlinearities) rather than multiple perceptrons
a_j = sum_i w_ji x_i + w_j0 are activations; z_j = h(a_j) are hidden units; w_ji weights, w_j0 biases
counts the layers of adaptive weights
a two-layer network with linear outputs can uniformly approximate any continuous function on a compact domain given enough hidden units
distinct weight vectors giving the same mapping: M! interchanges times 2^M sign flips
natural pairing of output activation and error function giving dE/da_k = y_k - t_k
batch uses the whole training set per step; on-line (sequential, stochastic) updates from one data point at a time
used specifically for the evaluation of derivatives, distinct from the weight-update stage
delta_j = dE_n/da_j
J_ki = dy_k/dx_i
second derivatives of error w.r.t. weights, W x W
H ~ sum_n b_n b_n^T, neglecting the (y_n - t_n) grad grad y_n term
quadratic regularizer (lambda/2) w^T w, negative log of a zero-mean Gaussian prior
halt training at the minimum of validation-set error
regularizer penalising change in output along the tangent of a transformation manifold
Omega = 1/2 integral ||grad y(x)||^2 p(x) dx, arises from input noise
(i) local receptive fields, (ii) weight sharing, and (iii) subsampling
mixture-of-Gaussians prior on weights so groups of weights take similar values (Nowlan and Hinton 1992)
mixture model for p(t|x) whose mixing coefficients, means and variances are outputs of a neural network
gamma = sum_i lambda_i/(alpha + lambda_i)

problems: Equations and superscripts are flattened by extraction (M!2M for M!2^M, O(W 2) for O(W^2)); symbols are transcribed in plain text in the JSON.

Inconsistencies in the book text: p. 245 Sec 5.3.2 calls tanh hidden units 'logistic sigmoid activation functions'; p. 239 Fig 5.6 caption says lengths are inversely proportional to square roots of 'eigenvectors' (should be eigenvalues); p. 262 says approach 2 (tangent propagation) is 'closely related to approach 2' (should be approach 1, augmentation); p. 254 Eq 5.95 uses H_kk' where M_kk' is defined in 5.92; p. 271 Eq 5.142 has indices mu_i - w_j swapped (should be w_i - mu_j); p. 275 Eq 5.153 sums k=1 to lowercase k; MDN output count text (K widths) disagrees with total (K+2)L.
Fig 5.10 is said to use 'polynomial data set' while text p. 256 cites the sinusoidal data of Fig 5.9.
